utterances.text: Yes. That's the portion of his statement that I also read to you from the English. Dr. Nakas, can you comment on what I just read what was said by the RS Minister of Health, Dragan Kalinic, and whether this was consistent with what you heard in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That is more or less an explanation of the statement which we heard at the meeting of the Crisis Staff about the necessity of destroying the Kosevo Hospital and making it impossible to use the medical resources in the surrounded city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you remember, more or less, when this meeting you discussed was?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: It was in the summer, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document is marked for identification so I would just leave it. And I note in e-court that the parties are supposed to agree about which parts of the document to be -- to tender. So we will make sure that, of course, these pages, meaning pages 19 to 21 of the B/C/S, and 17 to 19 of the English, will be part of the portions that we want to submit. But if you believe that it is better to tender this as separate exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think on the 1st of November we decided that we'll wait what will be used and that, finally, in order to avoid that we have the totality of a document in evidence --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we leave it as it is, and you keep record of what you have used so that you can agree with the Defence on it later --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, we will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, in several parts of your statement, you discuss the shelling and the sniping that hit the State Hospital at different points in time, and you also state that this fire, this shelling, sniper fire, emanated from the areas of Trebevic, Osmice, Vrace, and Grabovica, which were under the control of the Army of the Republika Srpska. And I read this from your statement at paragraphs 21, 25, 30 to 33. Now, can I ask you, what's the basis of your conclusion that the shelling of the fire was the responsibility of the Army of the Republika Srpska, was coming from the areas under their control?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Well, the foundation of such a statement of mine was based on several facts. One fact was well-known to everyone, including the UNPROFOR and international community; namely, that from May 1992 onwards, this area was under the control of the Serbian forces and the former Yugoslav People's Army. The second fact was that I personally saw tank shells being fired from Vrace and hitting Marin Dvor, including the military hospital, that is to say, the State Hospital in Sarajevo. My secretary was wounded by a shot which was probably fired from a sniper, and, after that, a similar shot hit my office. That convinced me that this was the location from which the majority of mortar fire came, as well as the majority of the projectiles that landed on the State Hospital. Likewise, the fact that everyone in the city and everyone else was well informed about the so-called "Sniper Alley," that was Trscanska Street which directly opens onto the State Hospital from Marsala Tita Street, and it made sniper fire possible in many ways. So these were the various elements that led me to make such an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question to clarify your second -- the second element that made you have -- conclude -- made you -- had such a conclusion. You say -- when you say you personally saw this fire or some tanks -- shells being fired, from where did you observe this? Where were you located when you -- you saw what you described.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: During the first two months after we had made it possible for the State Hospital to function, due to frequent shellings, most of what we had was moved from upper floors to the basement. However, I insisted that my office remain where the former office of the director of the former military hospital used to be. That is, on the third floor in the policlinic administration building of the State Hospital in Sarajevo. From my room, I had direct access to a terrace which faces Trebevic, Vrace, and Osmice. And on a daily basis, I had an opportunity to look from this terrace or through the open window or open door, and I could watch the firing from that direction and the other activities that were going on there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will move to another area and I will be seeking your help to clarify or interpret certain medical records.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have on the screens, well, it's now marked with exhibit number P951. This was one of the associated exhibits to the witness statement. This is a criminal investigation file relating to the 18th of November, 1994, sniping incident, and in the report there's medical documentation of the victims. It is the Scheduled Incident F12.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, I would now ask your help to clarify a diagnosis in this document or the way of reading the descriptions that we find in medical records.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we first go to e-court page 4 of the English and 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Dr. Nakas, you're familiar with this type of investigation reports; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the standard format of an official report drawn up by police investigators who conducted certain examination and then drew up Official Notes on unfortunate events. Sometimes they would draw them up in my office, and, on other occasions, I had the chance to see them when they came by to check whether some of the persons who were investigated into were treated at the State Hospital, were still there, and then we would, together, compare the findings and the state of health of such patients. So this is a form of official report that I'm quite familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Nakas, in this incident of the 18th of November, 1994, a woman and her son were hit by sniper fire. If you can please look towards the end of page 5 of the B/C/S, meaning the page that is now on your screens, I will read for you what the report of the security service centre, CSB, in Sarajevo says. For us, on the English, the part is the penultimate paragraphs. So the report says: "The interview conducted at the Sarajevo KCU administrations and triage dispensary yielded information that the wounded woman, Dzenana Sokolovic, had received an entry-and-exit wound in the abdominal area and was admitted for treatment at the KCU abdominal clinic. The entry wound is on the right, and the exit wound on the left side of the abdomen." And I will stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now can we please go to e-court page 6 of the English and 10 of the B/C/S. This is a letter of discharge issued by the Sarajevo medical centre for Ms. Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, can you please read the diagnosis for this patient and tell us what it means. If it's visible on the B/C/S. I see it's a poor copy.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It is visible. It says vulnus transsclopetarium tegmenti abdominis, which means that it is an entry/exit wound caused by a fire-arm on the abdominal wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we now move to page 7 of the English and 11 of the B/C/S. And if we can zoom in towards the end of the diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, I want to direct your attention to the part of the medical record that says: "Entry point of wound, 0.5 centimetres wide, to the paramedian left, bleeding, and exit point wound, 3 times 2 centimetres, to the paramedian right and bleeding." Can you please clarify what this means in layman's terms.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: In Latin, when you say "median," that means that we're talking about the central line that goes through our body. It's the middle part of our body from the head to the lower extremities. Paramedian means that something is next to that central line, not very far from it, not placed laterally but very close to the median line. It says here that one can see the entry wound on the left side, and on the right side there is an exit wound. Both wounds are bleeding. There is blood coming from both of the wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And I note that we just read, if you remember, from the CSB report that the entry wound was on the right side of the victim and the exit wound on the left side of the abdomen of the victim. How would you explain this, in conjunction with what the medical report says?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. These are questions for an expert witness, not a fact witness. Especially bearing in mind that the medical documentation was issued by the hospital where the witness that we are seeing today did not work at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Shall I repeat the question, Dr. Nakas.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, please. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. We just saw -- I just read from the medical report that the entry wound was on the paramedian left, and the exit wound to the paramedian right. And then I asked if you remember that just some minutes ago I read from the CSB report that the entry wound -- of course, we're talking about the same victim. The entry wound was on the right side of the victim and the exit wound was on the left side of the abdomen of the victim. And I asked you, whether -- as a doctor, when you read such a diagnosis or such an explanation, how can you explain the two documents together?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, objectively speaking, when you read both of these documents, you will arrive at a conclusion that they differ in one important fact. In one document, the entry wound is found on the right-hand side, where in the other document it is found on the left-hand side. Bearing in mind the circumstances surrounding all of the developments in the city of Sarajevo, which was encircled, and the burden suffered by those people who were working on treating all those who were wounded and who were sick at the time, mistakes were certainly possible. Even today, we can see that in the United States of America and in Sweden, there are trials conducted against hospitals where a healthy kidney was removed instead of a sick kidney or a healthy leg was operated upon instead of a -- a -- a sick leg. Mistakes are possible. Mis-recording of wounds is possible. And it was particularly prominent when there was no time or technical capabilities to produce accurate records. The most accurate record would be a photo that would confirm the accuracy of either one or the other document. Unfortunately, at that time, there was no time to make photo documentation of all the cases that we saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: You just discussed the -- the burden, the difficult circumstances suffered by those that were treating the wounded in -- well, in the -- in those days, in those years in Sarajevo. Can I ask you whether, considering the circumstances, this diagnosis of paramedian, right or left, could be based upon the view of the examiner looking at the patient? Meaning the doctor making the diagnosis by looking at the patient, so that the perspective would be the opposite?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness is asked to speculate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What caused the mistake. The witness has explained that mistakes are made, and we leave it to that at this moment. Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honours. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, in your statement, for example, paragraphs 67 to 68, you describe also the incident of the 28th of June, 1995, when the Radio Television centre was hit by an air bomb. In describing the injuries of those who received the medical assistance in your hospital, you say that there were also injuries caused by the blast syndrome, meaning injuries suffered to internal organs, in which there is air -- due to the increased air pressure of the explosion -- due to the explosion. This is in your statement. That's why I am recalling this. Can you explain us the difference between a blast injury and the blast syndrome.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The blast syndrome is a combination of symptoms that appear in people who are exposed to a direct explosion. It's something that medical professionals come across quite often, and we learn about it during our studies. It's a syndrome that we come across during peace time and especially during war time. Explosions cause certain injuries in the hollow organs within the organism resulting in damage to the lungs, abdomen, ears, and all the other cavities that are filled with air. Due to a blast, heart can stop working which leads to a sudden death. There may be other injuries such as bleeding in the central nervous system, or lungs, or the stomach. So this is a combination of symptom, and depending on the power of the blast and the impact on various types -- parts of the body, can have all sorts of different manifestations.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And these last ones you described would be the blast injuries, I take it.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. These would be the so-called blast injuries, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Doctor, do you remember viewing also medical records for the victims for the two Markale market incidents, the first on the 5th of February, 1994, and the second one on 28th of August, 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have on the screen 65 ter 10094. For the record this is also part of the document chart that I will later discuss with the witness and it's document 6 on the chart. Can we please go to e-court page 2 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: These are post-mortem records from the Kosevo Hospital of people killed at the Markale market incident on 5 -- on the 5th of February, 1994. Dr. Nakas, do you remember reviewing these -- this autopsy -- this post-mortem records in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, these are excerpts from autopsies which were carried out at the school of medicine in Sarajevo. They were performed at the Department of Forensic Medicine in Sarajevo. The documents provide the name, the diagnosis, the injuries, and the causes of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: There's also a statement to the fact that the autopsies were carried out by forensic medical experts, in order to establish the death -- the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The documents were all signed by Professor Ilijas Dobraca.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to comment on the diagnosis of this autopsy report that we see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The diagnosis is in Latin, and it reads: "Amputatio explosiva extremitatis inferioris." In translation this would mean amputation of lower extremities caused by explosion. The findings point out that the lower extremities were amputated by explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we now move to the next page. I have one following-up question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to finish on this document and then we can take the break. We can adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yeah, we're now on page 3 of both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And again, Dr. Nakas, I wanted to ask you if you can quickly comment just on the diagnosis, not on the rest of the document.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: It is the blast syndrome. This is the diagnosis. And in addition to that, there is also the diagnosis of vulnus explosivium capitis, thoracis, abdominis et extremitatis inferioris. The final diagnosis is the destructio explosiva pedis sinistri. In other words, this was a blast syndrome and explosive wounds on the head, the thorax, the abdomen, and both extremities. And, as a result there was a complete destruction of the foot of the left leg caused by explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. I take this last point is in conjunction with the previous elements, with the previous injuries already noted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This was your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask whether these injuries or causes of death that we notice in the majority of these autopsy reports are consistent with the explosion of a mortar or shell, in your opinion, for what you can see -- say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Again, the expert is asked to provide an expert opinion -- or, rather, the witness is required to provide an expert opinion, and this is our main objection to the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I was just asking for the medical observations with regard to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you're asking for medical opinion on whether it's consistent with. Now, you could even say that if your left foot is totally destroyed, if you have explosive wounds on your head, on your body, on your -- and if -- on your extremities, then it comes close to what is common knowledge, I would say. There's no need for the witness to answer the question, I would say. Facts of common knowledge do not need any proof. Ms. D'Ascoli, could you tell us whether this was your last question of your examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, not the last question of the examination. The last question for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you indicated that you would need one hour. You are beyond that already. So, therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 minutes was then extended to one hour. You're now over one hour. You're approximately at 64, 65 minutes, and therefore you should consider whether there are really -- I mean, and translation exercise in Latin is, of course, not what we really need. It's certainly a matter to be discussed with the Defence. I mean, the diagnosis, all of that, is just ordinary language.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. But I do have other areas to cover, Your Honours. And I believe that most of today was used also for procedural matters and for the admission of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is included in the time schedules. We'll consider. But please prepare for very limited time tomorrow, if at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nakas, I'd like to instruct you, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow at 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I. And you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 14th of February, at 9.30 in the morning, in this same Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of February, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.
